questions.title: Explain the CSS Box Model and how box-sizing affects it.
questions.description:
CSS Box Model

The CSS box model is a container that wraps around every HTML element. It consists of: margin, border, padding, and the actual content.

  • Content: The text or images inside the box.
  • Padding: Clear area around the content. Inside the border.
  • Border: Border that goes around the padding and content.
  • Margin: Clear area outside the border.

The box-sizing Property

By default (box-sizing: content-box), width and height apply only to the content box. Under box-sizing: border-box, width and height include content, padding, and border.
questions.bestPractices:
• Use box-sizing: border-box globally to make layout sizing predictable.
  • Avoid mixing absolute units (like pixels) with relative layouts unless necessary.
questions.commonMistakes:
• Forgetting that padding and borders add to the total width of an element, causing container overflow.
  • Using margins for spacing inside borders.
questions.example:
/* Apply border-box globally */
*,
*::before,
*::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

.card {
  width: 300px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 5px solid #000;
  /* Total width is exactly 300px, not 350px! */
}
questions.interviewTip: Explain why border-box is preferred (predictability) and write the global reset snippet from memory. Be sure to note that margins are not included in the width calculation of the box model.
followUpQuestions: What is the difference between margin collapsing and regular margins?
How does outline differ from border?

questions.title: What is CSS Specificity and how is it calculated?
questions.description:
CSS Specificity

Specificity is the algorithm used by browsers to determine which CSS rule applies to an element when multiple rules conflict. It is represented as four numbers or columns: inline styles, IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, and elements/pseudo-elements.

Calculation Hierarchy

  • Inline Styles (A): e.g., style="color: red" (Score: 1,0,0,0)
  • IDs (B): e.g., #header (Score: 0,1,0,0)
  • Classes, Attributes, and Pseudo-classes (C): e.g., .menu, [type="text"], :hover (Score: 0,0,1,0)
  • Elements and Pseudo-elements (D): e.g., div, ::before (Score: 0,0,0,1)
questions.bestPractices:
• Keep specificity low to make your CSS maintainable and reusable.
  • Avoid using !important. If you must use it, document why.
  • Use CSS variables for easy overrides instead of fighting specificity.
questions.commonMistakes:
• Relying on deep nesting (e.g. body header nav ul li a) which inflates specificity.
  • Using !important to fix specificity issues, which leads to stylesheets that are impossible to maintain.
questions.example:
/* Spec: 0, 1, 0, 0 (High) */
#title { color: blue; }

/* Spec: 0, 0, 1, 1 (Medium) */
.main-heading h1 { color: green; }

/* Spec: 0, 0, 0, 1 (Low) */
h1 { color: red; }

/* #title wins! */
questions.interviewTip: If given a set of selectors, calculate their specificity scores using the 4-number system. Emphasize that specificity takes precedence over order in source file.
followUpQuestions: Does the :where() pseudo-class add to specificity?
